payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
These are notes, not articles. Short pieces, each taking one idea as far as it goes, working out a single argument in public and in sequence. If you landed on one of them cold, this page is the map.

What a note is

A note is a short read, usually three to six minutes, that holds one idea and stops. It is not news commentary, and it is not written for search engines. Each one stakes a position and shows its work.

Once a note is published and dated, it does not get edited. There is one canonical version, and it stays the version it was the day it went up. If the thinking moves, that becomes a new note, not a quiet revision of an old one. You can trust that what you are reading is what was argued, when it was argued.

This page is the one exception. It describes the system, so it stays current.

How you can check

A promise that nothing gets edited is only as good as your willingness to believe me. The notes carry proof instead. Every one of them has a hash of its text anchored into the public Bitcoin ledger on the day it publishes. The badge at the top links to the block it landed in. Below the text sit a downloadable proof file and a public git ledger of every record, along with a page that walks through the check without taking my word for any of it.

This page carries more than one entry in that ledger, because this page is allowed to change, and the record shows exactly when it did.

Arguing that music needs proof of origin while publishing unprovable claims about my own work would be a strange way to make the case.

Why they exist

The notes are building one case. Music is heading into an era where the question of who made what, and with which inputs, decides who gets paid. The current answer is detection, which guesses after the fact and can always be challenged. The argument here is that the answer has to be provenance instead. Identity that is cryptographic, bound to the work, and signed at the moment of creation, so it survives the life of the file.

The formal versions of this argument live as papers. The notes are where it gets worked out in the open, one piece at a time, where anyone can follow the reasoning and push on it.

What provenance means here

The word is carrying two different questions right now, and they often get the same name.

Authorship provenance is about origin: who made a work, and when. It is settled once, at the moment the work is made, and the answer stays bound to it for the rest of its life. The other kind, behavioral provenance, is about conduct over time. Does a system keep doing what it said it would? That answer can change, so the checking never stops.

Everything here sits in the first regime. A finished recording does not start behaving differently three weeks after release, so what it needs is one honest proof of origin at creation, carried forward from there. Collapsing the two is how a research program gets dismissed by people who have not read it closely.

How they are organized

The notes sit in one index, newest first, each tagged by topic. Tags are the map. Follow one and you get every note that touches that thread. Some notes build on earlier ones and link back when they do, but there is no required order. Each one stands on its own.

Above the notes sit the pillar essays, the long-form anchors. Two of them have an academic paper behind them and hold the numbered spine, № 1.00 and № 2.00. № 1.01 extends the first into ground the paper did not cover, so it is numbered as a child of that argument rather than as a new one. A note assumes you have read the pillars, or are willing to.

Where to start

Start with the pillars. Provenance Over Detection carries the core argument. Cheap option extends it into the economics, which is where the case stops being a preference and becomes a cost comparison. Provenance as Substrate carries the technical case underneath both. Every note hangs off one of the three. From there, jump to whichever question brought you here, or work through the index and watch the argument accumulate.

How to follow

There is a feed, and the feed is the spine of all of it. Subscribe via RSS and new notes arrive as they publish. If you would rather read by email, point a service like Blogtrottr or Feedrabbit at the feed and each note lands in your inbox, on your account, not a list of mine. There is no signup form here and no list I keep, by design. The work is here for anyone who wants it, on the reader's terms.

Nothing here is finished. That is the reason for working it out where you can watch it happen.
